quoted_clause: If the architecture calls for data-parallel training of a 70B FP16 model across 8 nodes (an eight-rank DP group, e.g. one rank per node), the all-reduce bandwidth dictates whether the nodes are connected by InfiniBand, 200 GbE, or even 100 GbE.

correction: Either use a model that fits one rank (e.g., a smaller model) or define each DP rank as a multi-GPU model-parallel replica that fits, and state the all-reduce volume for that replica. Label the example communication-only and not memory-feasible if retained.

quoted_clause: each stage also carries its own activation memory, so per-stage memory cost bounds P from below
observed: The sentence says activation memory per stage bounds the number of pipeline stages P from below. In pipeline parallelism, per-stage activation memory primarily bounds the number of in-flight micro-batches m (or total activation memory), while weight memory per stage is what forces a minimum P. Increasing P does not reduce per-stage activation memory in the simple model.
evidence: The chapter's own pipeline model uses P stages and m micro-batches; activation memory is associated with micro-batches in flight, not with the number of stages. The statement conflates weight residency and activation residency.
root_cause: Weight-memory and activation-memory constraints are conflated in the mini-case.
correction: Distinguish: total weight memory bounds P from below (enough stages to hold weights); per-stage activation memory bounds m from above (or total in-flight memory), not P from below. Rewrite the parenthetical accordingly.
acceptance_test: The corrected sentence states a dimensionally and causally correct constraint: weight memory → minimum P; activation memory → maximum m or total memory budget.

quoted_clause: Memory fit: 140 GB weights + 24 GB KV = 164 GB < 640 GB aggregate
observed: The 164 GB check is a single-request residency check, not the workload memory gate. At the canonical 10 rps average and 8.6 s service time, Little's Law gives ~86 in-flight requests; 86 × 24 GB ≈ 2,064 GB KV for Candidate (a), and 86 × 1.2 GB ≈ 103 GB KV for Candidate (c). A single 640 GB host or 80 GB H100 therefore does not hold the workload's KV population. At 40 rps peak, ~344 in-flight requests imply ~8.3 TB and ~413 GB respectively.
evidence: Little's Law L = λW: 10 × 8.6 = 86; 40 × 8.6 = 344. Candidate (a) KV is 24 GB/request; Candidate (c) is 1.2 GB/request. The text itself later uses ~17.5 KV-resident requests per host and ~6 average / ~21 peak hosts, which contradicts calling the one-request 164 GB check a passing workload memory gate.
root_cause: Conflates single-request residency with the workload-level memory gate; the three-gate definition mixes per-unit and workload-level checks.
correction: Define the memory gate at workload concurrency, or explicitly separate 'single-request residency' from 'workload KV residency'. State that Candidate (a) as a one-host deployment fails workload KV residency at average and peak; Candidate (c) as a one-card deployment also fails at average concurrency. Recompute host/card counts from KV capacity, not only prefill throughput.
acceptance_test: Recompute 10 × 8.6 × 24 = 2,064 GB and 40 × 8.6 × 24 = 8,256 GB for (a); 10 × 8.6 × 1.2 = 103.2 GB and 40 × 8.6 × 1.2 = 412.8 GB for (c). Update Candidate (a)/(c) verdicts, Table 12-1 '✓ memory' cells, and mini-case 'fits the memory budget' statements so no single host/card is called memory-feasible for the workload.

quoted_clause: This is the number that, multiplied by the number of devices in the candidate layout, must exceed the workload's tokens-per-second demand
observed: The statement ignores parallelism topology. For TP/PP, devices cooperate on the same token stream, so aggregate throughput is not N × per-device throughput. The chapter itself says an 8×H100 TP=8 host sustains ~19,800 prefill tokens/s, not 8 × 19,780 ≈ 158,240.
evidence: Ch 12 §3: 'host aggregate is the same ~19,800 — not 8× a per-GPU rate'; 989 TFLOP/s × 35% ÷ 17.5 GFLOP/token = 19,780 per GPU, but TP=8 shares the token stream. Only data-parallel replicas multiply throughput.
root_cause: Generic 'per-device × devices' capacity rule applied without distinguishing DP replicas from TP/PP model-parallel groups.
correction: Replace with: aggregate goodput = number of independent replicas × per-replica goodput; within a TP/PP replica, devices do not multiply token rate. Add a worked check using the 70B TP=8 host.
acceptance_test: Revise §4 item 3 and verify no example computes 8 × 19,780 for the 70B TP=8 host; the 8×H100 host must remain ~19,800 prefill tokens/s.

quoted_clause: All three numbers must be confirmed before a candidate is carried forward. If any one fails, the candidate is returned to the synthesis step.

This directly contradicts 'if any one fails, returned to synthesis.'
evidence: §3 says Candidate (a) 'fails the throughput gate too'; Candidate (b) 'still fails the throughput gate at a single prefill host'; §6 says (a)/(b) 'carry forward as conditional finalists.'
root_cause: Undefined 'conditional finalist' / open-gate status conflicts with a strict all-gates-must-pass rule.
correction: Either (i) define conditional finalists as candidates with open gates that are advanced to measurement, and rewrite §4 to say 'a candidate with a failed gate is returned; a candidate with an unmeasured gate may advance as conditional'; or (ii) return (a)/(b) to synthesis. Make the same rule apply to (c).
acceptance_test: A single gate-status table in §4/§6/Table 12-1 uses one vocabulary (pass/fail/open) and no candidate is both 'failed' and 'carried forward' without an explicit conditional-finalist definition.

quoted_clause: 17.5 GFLOP/token per GPU
observed: The 14 and 17.5 GFLOP/token figures are linear 2N terms only. At the canonical 9.2K context, attention adds ~4.8 GFLOP/token for the 7B (32 layers, 4096 hidden) and ~24.1 GFLOP/token full-model for the 70B (80 layers, 8192 hidden), i.e. ~3.0 GFLOP/token per GPU under TP=8. Total prefill is ~18.8 GFLOP/token for 7B and ~20.5 GFLOP/token per GPU for 70B. At 35% MFU the rates are ~18.4K and ~16.9K tokens/s, not ~24.7K and ~19.8K.
evidence: Attention FLOPs per sequence = 4 × n_layers × L² × d_model; per token = 4 × n_layers × L × d_model. 7B: 4 × 32 × 9,200 × 4,096 ≈ 4.82 GFLOP/token. 70B: 4 × 80 × 9,200 × 8,192 ≈ 24.1 GFLOP/token full-model, ÷8 ≈ 3.0 per GPU. 989 TFLOP/s × 0.35 = 346.15 TFLOP/s; ÷18.82 GFLOP = 18,393 tok/s; ÷20.5 GFLOP = 16,885 tok/s.
root_cause: Using the 2N per-token approximation for prefill without stating it or adding the context-length-dependent attention term; the canonical 9.2K context makes the omission material.
correction: Either include the attention term in the prefill FLOP/token calculation or explicitly label the 2N figures as a linear-only lower bound and propagate the sensitivity. Recompute the 70B and 7B prefill rates and all host/card counts in Table 12-2.
acceptance_test: Recompute with 2N + 4 n_layers L d_model per token (or per-sequence equivalent) and show updated rates/host counts; if retaining 2N, add a sentence that the numbers are lower bounds and show the attention-inclusive values.

quoted_clause: An 8×H100 host (640 GB) fits this with ample headroom for concurrency (Ch11 showed ~24 GB per request × concurrent requests still fits).
observed: At the canonical ~17.5 KV-resident requests per host, 140 GB weights + 17.5 × 24.9 GB KV + ~64 GB runtime ≈ 639.75 GB, i.e. zero headroom. Ch 12 §3 Candidate (b) itself says 'exactly the pool, zero headroom.' 'Ample headroom' is only true for a single request.
evidence: 140 + 17.5 × 24.9 + 64 = 639.75 GB; 640 − 639.75 = 0.25 GB. The text's own 24.9 GB/request and 17.5 requests/host imply zero headroom.
root_cause: Inconsistent KV-per-request basis (24 vs 24.9 GB) and failure to include weights/runtime when saying 'ample headroom for concurrency.'
correction: Replace 'ample headroom for concurrency' with 'zero headroom at the canonical 17.5-request concurrency; ample only for a single request' or reduce the KV budget/runtime assumption and show the arithmetic.
acceptance_test: The sentence and any adjacent table show 140 + 17.5 × 24.9 + 64 ≈ 640 GB and do not claim ample concurrency headroom.

quoted_clause: If not, the floor is a cluster.

evidence: Ch 13 §2: 'KV residency per GPU: model + KV no longer fits one GPU → single host'; 'Memory: model + KV no longer fits one node → cluster.'

correction: Rewrite: 'The 4-bit KV cache is intended as a memory optimization; it is not quality-neutral and can add its own quality penalty, which must be validated.'
acceptance_test: The sentence no longer says both 'not a quality one' and 'can add a quality penalty' without qualification.

quoted_clause: Server | 1-8 | scale-up fabric (NVLink/NVSwitch) | ~70-180B dense
observed: The row can be read as saying a 1-GPU server serves 70-180B dense. At FP16, 70B is 140 GB, which does not fit one 80 GB GPU. The range applies only at the upper end of the 1-8 GPU count (and with enough aggregate memory).
evidence: 70B × 2 bytes = 140 GB > 80 GB; 8×H100 = 640 GB. The text itself says 13B FP16 = 26 GB exceeds many edge GPUs.
root_cause: Tier-level model range not qualified by GPU count/precision.
correction: Add 'at the upper GPU counts and appropriate precision' or split the row into 1-GPU and 8-GPU server subcases.
acceptance_test: Table 13-1 no longer implies a 1-GPU server can hold a 70B FP16 dense model.

quoted_clause: On the compute axis a single host also serves only ~19.8K of the ~92K input tokens/s the 10 rps average needs (~5 hosts, Ch12/8), so the peak failure is a compute shortfall, not merely queueing delay.
observed: The sentence uses the 10 rps average demand (~92K) to explain a 40 rps peak failure. At peak the demand is ~368K input tokens/s and the prefill screen is ~19 hosts, not ~5. The conclusion (compute shortfall at peak) is true, but the cited arithmetic is for average load.
evidence: 10 × 9.2K = 92K; 40 × 9.2K = 368K. Ch 12 Table 12-2 gives ~19 prefill hosts at peak.
root_cause: Average/peak demand conflation in the explanatory clause.
correction: Use the peak numbers: 'at 40 rps the input demand is ~368K tokens/s, so even the prefill screen needs ~19 hosts; the peak failure is a compute shortfall as well as queueing delay.'
acceptance_test: The sentence cites 368K and ~19 hosts when explaining peak failure, or explicitly says 'even at average load...'.

quoted_clause: Data residency / sovereignty — data must not leave the facility or the jurisdiction — forces the on-prem server (or cluster) tier
observed: Data residency/sovereignty requires data to remain in a jurisdiction, not necessarily on-prem. An in-country cloud region can satisfy it. The sentence overstates the constraint.
evidence: The clause itself says 'facility or jurisdiction'; jurisdiction can be satisfied by a compliant cloud region.
root_cause: Equating data residency with on-premises deployment.
correction: Say 'forces an in-jurisdiction deployment, which may be on-prem or a compliant cloud region; if the requirement is facility-level, it forces on-prem.'
acceptance_test: The paragraph distinguishes jurisdiction residency from facility-level on-prem requirements.

quoted_clause: Contention / phase interference: SLO can't be met because prefill and decode contend for the same resources → split prefill/decode (a within-tier move).
observed: P/D disaggregation typically requires separate prefill and decode pools/hosts, which can be a tier escalation (e.g., server → cluster), not merely a within-tier move. The chapter's own Candidate (b) uses two 8×H100 hosts.
evidence: Ch 12 Candidate (b): 'two hosts and added fabric as a baseline'; Ch 13 §1 cluster tier includes P/D disaggregation.
root_cause: Calling P/D disaggregation a within-tier move without specifying that it can be within a cluster tier or require additional hosts.
correction: Say 'split prefill/decode, which may be a within-tier reconfiguration if spare hosts exist or a tier escalation if it requires new pools/fabric.'
acceptance_test: The trigger description no longer implies P/D disaggregation is always within-tier.
